t: Aim and plan of the session
n: The aim of the session is to study the toxicological significance and analytical methods of indole derivatives that pass into the organic solvent in an acidic medium, that is, strychnine and brucine. The plan: the toxicological significance of the alkaloids strychnine and brucine and the methods of their analysis. In the DVSSM course package, reserpine is also included in the title of the session. Quantitative analysis is carried out by UV spectrophotometry.

Expected outcomes and equipment. Students master the conditions for detecting strychnine and brucine from pure solutions and from an unknown composition by qualitative reactions. Necessary items: test tubes, separating funnels, reagents, visual materials; the work is carried out in a specially equipped room. Alkaloid reagents are prepared fresh in the laboratory: this ensures that the reaction is performed accurately.

This is the session map. The plan covers the toxicological significance and analytical methods of the alkaloids strychnine and brucine. First, the alkaloid reagents are prepared fresh in the laboratory: the Dragendorff, Bouchardat, Mayer, Scheibler, Mandelin, Erdmann and Marquis reagents. Then the reactions of strychnine and brucine are performed. Quantitative analysis is carried out by UV spectrophotometry, that is, a spectrophotometer, and by the PEC method. UV maxima: strychnine 255 nm; brucine 267 and 301 nm; brucine in TLC Rf = 0.21.

General understanding of alkaloids. The word "alkaloid" means "alkali-like"; the first representative was isolated in 1819. Alkaloids occur mainly in plant organs, and most have strong pharmacological action. In base form almost all are crystalline, poorly soluble in water and readily soluble in organic solvents; some are liquids.

The general precipitating reagents for alkaloids fall into two groups: those forming simple salts and those forming complex compounds. Those forming simple salts include tannin, KMnO4, picric and picrolonic acids, and chromates. Complex-forming reagents are either metalloid-containing: I2/KI, Br2/KBr, Sonnenschein's and Scheibler's; or metal-containing: Marmé's, Mayer's, Dragendorff's, HgCl2, K3[Fe(CN)6]. Scheibler's, Sonnenschein's and Dragendorff's reagents and picric and picrolonic acids are sensitive reagents, so their negative result is important.

Colour reagents. As colour reagents, nitric, hydrochloric and sulphuric acids and their mixtures are used. Erdmann's reagent consists of sulphuric and nitric acid, Marquis of formaldehyde and sulphuric acid, and Fröhde's of ammonium molybdate and sulphuric acid. The Marquis reagent is a general reaction for morphine derivatives, the murexide reaction for purine derivatives, and cobalt ammoniate for barbiturates. Nitric acid gives a specific reaction for brucine, and hydrochloric, sulphuric and nitric acids for veratrine.

The difference between specific and selective reactions. Specific reactions are characteristic of one substance; other substances must not give them. Examples: blue colour of iodine with starch, the red precipitate of Cu2HgI4 for mercury, Prussian blue for hydrocyanic acid. In a selective reaction, however, one reagent gives a similar result with several substances: for example, FeCl3 for the phenolic hydroxyl, the azo dye for aniline derivatives.

One reaction is not enough. In the analysis of alkaloids, 2 or more reactions and methods must be used, without relying on one reaction. If the sensitivity of the reaction is low, a small amount of substance is not detected; if it is not specific, a wrong conclusion is drawn. Drawing a conclusion only from the Vitali–Morin reaction, only from the murexide reaction or only from the Marquis reagent is wrong, because other alkaloids give the same result: atropine, purine alkaloids and opium alkaloids.

Cadaveric alkaloids. As a result of putrefaction of the bio-object, foreign substances such as histidine and histamine are formed, which can give a precipitate like alkaloids. They are called "cadaveric alkaloids": cadaveric atropine, cadaveric nicotine, cadaveric strychnine. In the scheme, lysine, by decarboxylation, that is, losing CO2, becomes cadaverine; histamine is formed from histidine in this way. Although cadaveric atropine gives the Vitali–Morin reaction, it does not dilate the pupil; cadaveric nicotine has no pharmacological action.

Procedure for analysing alkaloids. First: isolation. Second: purification of the acidic and alkaline isolate by various methods. Third: testing with general precipitating and colour reagents. Fourth: physicochemical methods. Fifth: pharmacological testing for some alkaloids. Sixth: determination of the amount of the alkaloid detected. Remember: the chemist must use 2 or more reactions and methods, without relying on the result of one reaction.

Preparing the reagents, part one. Dragendorff's reagent, according to Munier: 0.85 g of basic bismuth nitrate is dissolved in 10 ml of glacial acetic acid and diluted with 40 ml of water. To it is added 20 ml of water in which 8 g of KI has been dissolved. From the solution obtained, 1 ml is taken and 2 ml of glacial acetic acid and 10 ml of water are added. Bouchardat's reagent: 2 g of KI is dissolved in 10–15 ml of water and 1.27 g of iodine is added; after dissolving, water is added to make 100 ml.

Preparing the reagents, part two. Mayer's reagent: 1.35 g of mercury(II) chloride is dissolved in 20 ml of 25% KI solution and made up to 100 ml with water. Scheibler's reagent: to 20 ml of 25% sodium tungstate, 10 ml of 25% phosphoric acid is added and mixed well.

Preparing the reagents, part three, that is, the colour reagents. Mandelin's reagent: to 0.01 g of ammonium vanadate, 2 ml of concentrated sulphuric acid is added and shaken. Erdmann's reagent: to 20 ml of concentrated sulphuric acid, 10 drops of 15% nitric acid are added and shaken. Marquis reagent: to 10 ml of concentrated sulphuric acid, 10 drops of formalin are added and the mixture is cooled.

Properties of strychnine. Strychnine occurs together with brucine in the kuchala plant, nux vomica and other plants; it is one of the most poisonous substances. In base form it is readily soluble in chloroform and ethyl alcohol and sparingly soluble in water and diethyl ether. Its nitrate dissolves in water, chloroform and alcohol; the sulphate dissolves readily in water and alcohol. It is isolated from the object with acidified water, alcohol and electrodialysis; it is extracted mainly under alkaline and partly under acidic conditions.

Poisoning with strychnine and metabolism. In poisoning, the central nervous system is excited and tetanic convulsions occur, rapidly reversible; death results from paralysis of the central nervous system. It is especially dangerous in diseases of the liver, kidneys and heart and in childhood diseases. Strychnine is absorbed quickly, about 80% undergoes metabolism, and the rest is excreted unchanged in the urine. It may accumulate in the body and persist in the organs of a corpse for several years.

Isolation and extraction of strychnine. Strychnine is isolated from a biological object by acidified water, acidified alcohol and electrodialysis. It passes into the organic solvent under both alkaline and acidic conditions, but the main part is extracted under alkaline conditions. Therefore strychnine is tested in the alkaline isolate. Its nitrate and the alcoholic solution of nux vomica, that is, chilibukha, are used in medicine.

Strychnine in medicine. In medicine, strychnine nitrate and the alcoholic solution of nux vomica, that is, chilibukha, are used. They are used in weakness, when blood pressure falls and when cardiac activity weakens. They are also used when metabolism falls, and in paresis and paralysis.

t: Amount of strychnine: the Malaken–Denije reaction
n: Amount of strychnine: the Malaken–Denije reaction. Strychnine is determined by the PEC method using the Malaken–Denije reaction. First, strychnine is reduced in the presence of HCl and Zn powder. If NaNO2 solution is added to the reduction product, a red colour forms. On this basis the intensity of the colour is measured on the PEC and the amount is determined photocolorimetrically.

Precipitation and dichromate reactions of strychnine. Strychnine forms a precipitate with reagents such as Dragendorff's, Mayer's, Scheibler's, Sonnenschein's, picric acid and tannin. In the dichromate reaction, the chloroform solution is evaporated in a porcelain dish. To the residue, 1–2 drops of conc. H2SO4 and 1–2 crystals of K2Cr2O7 are added and stirred with a glass rod. Result: a violet trace that quickly fades.

t: Strychnine: Mandelin's reagent and UV spectrum
n: Strychnine: Mandelin's reagent and UV spectrum. To the residue after evaporation of the chloroform isolate, in a porcelain dish, 1–2 drops of Mandelin's reagent are added. If strychnine is present, a blue-violet colour forms. In the UV spectrum, solutions of strychnine in ethyl alcohol and in 0.1 M sulphuric acid give a maximum at 255 nm.

t: Strychnine: TLC, pharmacological test and amount
n: Other tests for strychnine. By TLC, Rf = 0.33. In the pharmacological test, strychnine causes a state of tetanic convulsions in a frog. The amount is determined by the PEC method with the Malaken–Denije reaction: if, after reduction in HCl and Zn powder, NaNO2 is added to the product, a red colour forms.

Map of strychnine reactions. Precipitating reagents: a precipitate forms with Dragendorff's, Mayer's, Scheibler's and Sonnenschein's reagents, picric acid and tannin. Colour reactions: K2Cr2O7 + H2SO4 violet, fading quickly, and with Mandelin's reagent blue-violet. Physicochemical methods: TLC Rf = 0.33; UV spectrum: maximum at 255 nm in ethyl alcohol and in 0.1 M sulphuric acid. Pharmacological test: tetanic convulsions in a frog.

Properties and significance of brucine. Chemically, brucine is similar to strychnine and differs only by two methoxyl groups. In base form it is readily soluble in ethyl alcohol, chloroform and diethyl ether and poorly soluble in water. It is not used in medicine, and in practice it is used for detecting nitric acid. In poisoning with kuchala or preparations from it, it is detected from the bio-object; the main part undergoes metabolism.

Colour reactions of brucine. Brucine gives a red colour with SnCl2 and HNO3, whereas strychnine does not. With Sonnenschein's reagent it forms a colour that is first red and then turns yellow. With Erdmann's reagent it also gives a red colour, whereas strychnine does not. With the general precipitating reagents for alkaloids it forms a precipitate.

Brucine: microcrystals, TLC and UV. If 0.1 N HCl and 1% ammonium dichromate are added dropwise, light yellow prismatic crystals form; sensitivity 1.5 µg. In TLC with chloroform–acetone–diethylamine, in the ratio 50:30:2, and modified Dragendorff reagent, it gives a brown spot at Rf = 0.21. In the UV spectrum, the alcoholic solution gives a maximum at 267 and 301 nm, and the solution in 0.1 N H2SO4 at 265 and 300 nm.

Map of brucine reactions. Brucine forms a precipitate with the general precipitating reagents for alkaloids. Colour reactions: SnCl2 + HNO3 and Erdmann's reagent give a red colour, and Sonnenschein's reagent gives a colour changing from red to yellow. With ammonium dichromate, prismatic crystals form, sensitivity 1.5 µg. Physicochemical indices: TLC Rf 0.21; UV 267 and 301 nm.

Distinguishing strychnine and brucine. Brucine interferes with the dichromate reaction; therefore it is first destroyed with conc. H2SO4 and HNO3. Strychnine gives no colour with SnCl2 and HNO3 or with Erdmann's reagent, whereas brucine gives a red colour. The UV maximum in alcohol is 255 for strychnine and 267 and 301 nm for brucine. In TLC, the Rf is 0.33 for strychnine and 0.21 for brucine.

UV spectrum maxima. Solutions of strychnine in ethyl alcohol and in 0.1 M sulphuric acid give a maximum at 255 nm. The alcoholic solution of brucine gives a maximum at 267 and 301 nm. The solution of brucine in 0.1 N sulphuric acid forms spectra with maxima at 265 and 300 nm.

Distinguishing by TLC. The Rf value of strychnine in TLC is 0.33; the system is not given in the book. For brucine the mobile phase is chloroform–acetone–diethylamine, in the ratio 50:30:2, and the detecting reagent is modified Dragendorff reagent. Brucine forms a brown spot at Rf = 0.21.

Laboratory session 5 of the DVSSM course. Topic: preparing reagents in the analysis of alkaloids; detecting strychnine, brucine and reserpine in the isolate and in liquid materials. The reagents and the content of the strychnine and brucine reactions are the same as in the Pharmacy course package; quantitative analysis is carried out by UV spectrophotometry. By the Snowstorm method, three groups solve situational problems.

Reserpine: what the book gives. Reserpine is listed among the toxicologically significant alkaloids such as caffeine, quinine, morphine and strychnine. The title of the session names strychnine, brucine and reserpine, but the reactions described are only for strychnine and brucine. Hence the question: "Explain the specific method of analysing reserpine".

t: Basis of UV spectrophotometric quantitative analysis
n: Basis of UV spectrophotometric quantitative analysis. Spectrophotometry is based on determining monochromatic rays in the visible and the adjoining ultraviolet region. The absorbance of the solution is measured at the wavelength corresponding to the maximum absorption of the substance. The concentration is chosen so that the absorbance lies in the range from 0.2 to 1.0. The reference solution consists of all the components in the solution under test.

The spectrophotometric procedure in the book example. To prepare the standard, 0.1 g of substance is dissolved in ethyl alcohol in a 100 ml flask and made up to the mark. The absorption spectrum of the solution is measured at 200–400 nm. The absorbance of the isolated substance is measured at the maximum; ethyl alcohol is taken as the reference solution.

Methods of quantitative analysis. The amount of strychnine is determined by the PEC method, that is, with the Malaken–Denije reaction. The amount of brucine is determined by the PEC and spectrophotometer methods. In the DVSSM course package the title of the session is: quantitative analysis by UV spectrophotometry.

Situational tasks by the Snowstorm method. Group 1: when K2Cr2O7 and conc. H2SO4 were added to an isolate from internal organs obtained with acidified water, a bluish-violet and then a red colour appeared; find the substance. Group 2: is brucine used in medicine, what is its toxicological significance, and what is the specific method of analysing reserpine. Case 18: in the organs of a corpse, tetanic convulsions in the muscles were observed; for which substances should analysis be carried out.

Review questions. First: explain the toxicological significance and pharmacological action of strychnine. Second: how can strychnine be distinguished from brucine and separated from it. Third: how can the amount of indole alkaloids be determined. Fourth: what microcrystalline reactions exist for strychnine and brucine.

Continuation of the review questions. Write the formulae of the alkaloids containing an indole derivative. Characterise the reactions of strychnine with the general precipitating reagents and with H2SO4 in the presence of K2Cr2O7. Is brucine used in medicine; state its toxicological significance. How can salicylic acid be detected in blood and urine? Give a characteristic reaction for salicylic acid.

We conclude. Strychnine gives a violet colour in K2Cr2O7 + H2SO4, fading quickly, a blue-violet colour with Mandelin's reagent, and a UV maximum of 255 nm. Brucine gives a red colour with SnCl2 + HNO3 and Erdmann's reagent; Rf = 0.21; UV 267 and 301 nm. Quantitative analysis: strychnine is determined by the PEC method, that is, Malaken–Denije, and brucine by the PEC and spectrophotometer methods.
